## Plan

### Files that differ
1. `/workspace/attr/_make.py` vs `/megabit/.megabit_ref/attr/_make.py`
2. `/workspace/attr/__init__.py` vs `/megabit/.megabit_ref/attr/__init__.py`
3. `/workspace/tests/test_make.py` vs `/megabit/.megabit_ref/tests/test_make.py`
4. `/workspace/tests/test_funcs.py` vs `/megabit/.megabit_ref/tests/test_funcs.py`

### What I found
In the workspace today, the class decorator that adds the generated methods lives in `attr/_make.py` under the short public-sounding name `s`. In the reference, that same function is called `_add_methods` inside `attr/_make.py`, and `attr/__init__.py` gives the short name `s` to it by importing `_add_methods` and naming it `s`. The rest of the package is untouched: `_make_attr`, `_get_attrs`, and the four switch arguments (`add_repr`, `add_cmp`, `add_hash`, `add_init`) behave exactly the same in both versions, and `__all__` still lists `s` and `ib`.

### What is wrong for the user right now
- The name that describes what the decorator does (adding the generated methods) is not used anywhere in the package; only the one-letter shortcut is. Anyone reading `attr/_make.py` sees a bare `s` with no clue what it does.
- Inside the package the short name `s` is treated as an ordinary name, so it looks like a second public entry point sitting next to `ib` in the same file, which invites confusion about what people are meant to import from where.
- Reaching for the decorator by its short name inside the helper module (which the tests in `tests/test_make.py` and `tests/test_funcs.py` do today) is only possible because of the short name. Once the descriptive name is in place, anything that pulled the short name out of that helper module stops working, and those two test files are exactly where that has to be adjusted.

### What the ticket should say
- **What happens now:** the decorator that builds the printed form, equality, hashing and the initializer only exists inside the helper module under the one-letter name, and the descriptive name is nowhere to be found.
- **What should happen:** the helper module holds the decorator under a descriptive name, and the package still hands out the short one-letter name so every existing use of it keeps working without edits.
- **Problem this solves:** people reading the source have no idea what the one-letter decorator does, and there is no clear split between the name meant for use in the package's own files and the short name meant for user code.
- **User experience:** no visible difference for someone writing `attr.s` on their class — same short name, same behavior, same defaults. The only visible difference is for someone who reached into the helper module by the short name and now finds the descriptive name instead.

### Hints (workspace paths only)
- `/workspace/attr/_make.py`
- `/workspace/attr/__init__.py`
- `/workspace/tests/test_make.py`
- `/workspace/tests/test_funcs.py`

### Sections to write
Title, What happens now, What should happen, About this project, Problem this solves, What changed, Impact, User experience, Hints — in that order, no code, no developer jargon.

{"content":"# The decorator that builds the extra class methods has no readable name

## What happens now
If you open the file that builds the extra class methods, the one thing that attaches the printed form, the equality check, the hash and the initializer is called with a single letter. Nothing in the file says in words what that piece does, and the name that spells it out is not used anywhere in the project. The single letter is also what that file exports, which makes it hard to tell which name is meant for use inside the project and which name is meant for people writing their own classes.

## What should happen
The file that builds the extra class methods should carry that piece under a name that says in words that it adds those methods to your class. The short one-letter name should still be handed out by the package, so every existing use of it keeps working exactly as before.

## About this project
This is the attrs project, a small helper library for Python. You write down the fields your class should have and it creates the initializer, the printed form, the equality check and the hash for you, so you do not have to write those by hand.

## Problem this solves
Reading the source of the package today gives no hint about what the one-letter decorator does, so anyone trying to understand or reuse it has to read the whole body. Giving it a readable name inside the package removes that guesswork without asking anyone to change the code they already wrote.

## What changed
The decorator that attaches the extra methods now lives in the internal file under a spelled-out name instead of the single letter. The package still exports the short single-letter name for everyone who uses it from the top level, and nothing was removed: the same switches for the initializer, the printed form, equality and hashing all behave as before.

## Impact
Readability and naming inside the project. No speed change, no behavior change for people writing classes, and no change to the short name or to the four switches that turn the extra methods on and off.

## User experience
Before: you decorate your class with the short single-letter name, it works, and nothing about your code changes. But if you go into the package source to see what that single letter does, you find no readable name for it anywhere.

After: your code stays exactly as it was and keeps working the same way. The single letter still comes from the top level of the package. Inside the package source, the piece that adds the methods is now named in words, so you can tell at a glance what it does. The only thing that stops working is reaching into the internal file for the single letter, since that file now uses the readable name.

## Hints
- /workspace/attr/_make.py
- /workspace/attr/__init__.py
- /workspace/tests/test_make.py
- /workspace/tests/test_funcs.py
